Greenback mackerel Trachurus declivis reaches an ultimate total length of 64 cm [Li = 64 cm], making it one of the larger members of the Carangidae in Australian waters, a size attained through sustained somatic growth over several years. Field surveys have recorded adult individuals with a maximum wet weight of 2913 grams [Wwi = 2913 grams], a mass that is consistent with the allometric scaling relationships described for other pelagic carangids and reflects the substantial muscle mass necessary for sustained high-speed pursuit of prey. At the other end of the size spectrum, the pelagic eggs of this species, which measure approximately 1 mm in diameter, give rise to larvae with an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], a value derived from the spherical volume of the yolk-laden egg and representing the minimal energetic endowment before the onset of exogenous feeding. The contrast between the neonatal mass and the adult asymptotic mass underscores the extraordinary scope of post-embryonic growth that defines the life history of this pelagic teleost.

Life history data for Trachurus declivis indicate that the total length at puberty is 31.5 cm [Lp = 31.5 cm], a size attained when individuals transition from the pre-metamorphic larval phase into the sub-adult stage and begin vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis. This length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 355 grams [Wwp = 355 grams], calculated from length-weight regressions for this species and representing the energetic threshold above which resources are partitioned toward gamete production. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been estimated at 5% [GSI = 5%] for actively spawning individuals maintained at a water temperature of 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C].

The embryonic development of Greenback mackerel proceeds rapidly under cool-temperate conditions. At a constant incubation temperature of 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C], the time at birth, defined as the interval from gamete fusion to eclosion of the yolk-sac larva, is 4.55 days [ab = 4.55 days], a short developmental window typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts with small, transparent eggs. This rapid embryogenesis minimizes the duration of the vulnerable egg stage in the plankton, though it demands a relatively high yolk utilization rate to complete organogenesis before the chorion ruptures. The newly emerged prolarva, measuring only a few millimeters in length, is entirely lecithotrophic and remains dependent on endogenous yolk reserves for the first few days post-hatching. The combination of a small egg size, a brief incubation period, and a tiny larval mass at hatching reflects a classic r-selected reproductive strategy, in which high fecundity compensates for the elevated mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase.

Longevity data for this species, compiled from tag-recapture studies and otolith-based age determinations, indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of 25 years [am = 25 years] for individuals experiencing the ambient thermal regime of southeastern Australian waters at 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C]. This extended lifespan, exceeding that of many smaller carangids, is consistent with a relatively slow pace of life at high latitudes, where cooler temperatures depress metabolic rates and delay senescence. The oldest documented individuals are those that have matured slowly, invested modestly in annual reproduction, and avoided the high predation pressure that truncates survival in faster-growing cohorts. Comparative data across the genus Trachurus suggest that lifespan is positively correlated with ultimate body size, and Greenback mackerel, with its 64 cm asymptotic length, falls within the expected longevity range for a carangid of its dimensions. Field records also show that senescent fish exhibit declining condition factors and reduced gonadal investment in their final years.

The spawning phenology of Trachurus declivis is closely tied to seasonal temperature cycles along the continental shelf of southern Australia. Reproductive adults aggregate in mid-water during late spring and summer, with peak gamete release occurring when surface temperatures are near 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C], a thermal threshold that appears to synchronize gonadal recrudescence and final oocyte maturation across the population. Gravid individuals at this temperature exhibit a gonadosomatic index of 5% [GSI = 5%] at a temperature of 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C]. The resulting fertilized eggs, each containing a single yolk mass supporting the developing embryo, are broadcast into the plankton, where they complete their 4.55-day incubation (4.55 days) [ab = 4.55 days] before hatching at a temperature of 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C]. This thermal coupling of spawning and embryonic development ensures that larval emergence coincides with the seasonal peak in zooplankton abundance, thereby maximizing the probability of successful first feeding and subsequent recruitment into the adult population.
